title: Joining sentences
description: Connect ideas with and, but, or, because, so, if, when, before, after and 'that'.

guide.title: And, also, but, or
guide.text:
ಮತ್ತು (mattu) is 'and' between nouns: tee mattu kaafi. In speech it is often left out, or replaced by adding a long -oo to each item: ನಾನೂ ನೀವೂ (naanoo neevoo), 'both I and you'.

On a single word -oo means 'also, too': naanoo barteeni, 'I too will come'; idoo beku, 'I want this as well'.

To join two actions, Kannada does not use 'and' at all - it uses the 'having done' form: oota maadi banni, 'eat and come'.

ಆದ್ರೆ (aadre) is 'but'; the written form is ಆದರೆ (aadare).

ಅಥವಾ (athavaa) is 'or' in statements and choices. In everyday speech you also hear ಇಲ್ಲಾಂದ್ರೆ (illaandre), 'if not, otherwise'. For 'A or B?' questions remember the -aa ... -aa pattern: tee bekaa, kaafi bekaa?

examples.native: ಬರಬೇಕು ಅಂತ ಇದೆ, ಆದ್ರೆ ಸಮಯ ಇಲ್ಲ.
examples.roman: barabeku anta ide, aadre samaya illa.
examples.english: I'd like to come, but I have no time.

guide.title: Because and so
guide.text:
ಯಾಕಂದ್ರೆ (yaakandre), 'because', is literally 'if you say why'. It comes at the start of the reason, after the main statement, just as in English: naanu baralla, yaakandre kelasa ide. The written form is ಏಕೆಂದರೆ (ekendare).

More natural in Kannada is to give the reason first and then say ಅದಕ್ಕೆ (adakke), 'for that, so, that's why': nanage hushaarilla, adakke baralilla, 'I am unwell, that's why I didn't come'.

A reason can also be attached to a noun with -inda: maleyinda, 'because of the rain'.

examples.english: I won't come, because I have work.
I am unwell, so I didn't come.
I got late because of the rain.

guide.title: If
guide.text:
'If' is not a separate word but an ending on the verb: past stem + -ರೆ (-re). In speech: bandre (if ... come), hodre (if ... go), maadidre (if ... do), nodidre (if ... see), kotre (if ... give), idre (if ... is), aadre (if ... becomes - this is where 'but' comes from). Written forms keep an a: bandare, hodare, maadidare, iddare.

The form is the same for every person; the subject is shown by a pronoun: neevu bandre, 'if you come'; male bandre, 'if it rains'.

The 'if' clause comes first. For 'it would be good if ...' finish with chennaagirutte.

Negative 'if not': negative participle + idre: barade idre (ಬರದೆ ಇದ್ರೆ), 'if (you) don't come'. With nouns and adjectives use illaandre / illa andre, 'if not'.

gottidre (gottu + idre) is 'if (you) know'; bekaadre (beku + aadre) is 'if (you) want'; saadhya aadre, 'if possible'.

examples.english: If it rains, I won't come.
It would be nice if you came.

guide.title: When, after, before, until
guide.text:
These too are endings or words placed after a verb form - the time clause always comes first.

When: past stem + -ಆಗ (-aaga): bandaaga (when ... came / comes), hodaaga (when ... went), iddaaga (when ... was), nodidaaga (when ... saw). neevu bandaaga fon maadi, 'call when you come'.

After: past stem + -a + ಮೇಲೆ (mele): banda mele (after coming), hoda mele (after going), oota aada mele (after the meal is over).

Before: the -oke form (or the written -uva form) + ಮುಂಚೆ (munche): hogoke munche, 'before going'; oota maadoke munche, 'before eating'. With a noun, use the dative: ootakke munche, 'before the meal'.

Until: the spoken relative participle ('that comes' form) in -o + ತನಕ (tanaka): naanu baro tanaka, 'until I come'. baro is the spoken form of baruva, 'that comes'.

examples.english: Stay right here until I come.

guide.title: 'That': the quoting word anta
guide.text:
ಅಂತ (anta) is placed after anything said, thought, heard or known, and works like 'that' or like closing quotation marks. The quoted words come first and keep the form the original speaker used:

avaru 'naale barteeni' anta helidru - literally 'he "tomorrow I-will-come" thus said' = 'he said he would come tomorrow'. Notice that the verb inside stays barteeni ('I will come'), exactly as he said it.

It is used with heli (say), keli (ask), gottu (know), annisutte (seems), andkonde ('I thought'): avaru bartaare anta gottu, 'I know that they are coming'.

anta + ide after -beku expresses a wish: hogabeku anta ide, 'I feel like going'.

The written form of anta is ಎಂದು (endu).

examples.english: He said he would come tomorrow.
I know that they are coming.

phrases.english: I'd like to come, but I have no time.

It would be nice if you came.
I am unwell, so I didn't come.
I won't come, because I have work.
He said he would come tomorrow.
